design_detail: Retrospective single-centre case series of all adults admitted from the emergency department (ED) of one urban university-affiliated trauma centre (Hurley Medical Center, Flint, Michigan; annual ED census 55,000) with chest pain after recent cocaine use, 1 July 1996 to 28 February 1998. The Methods call it a retrospective cohort study (p. 873) and the Discussion a retrospective case series (p. 876); there is no comparison group. A departmental policy required admission of every patient with cocaine-associated chest pain for at least 23 hours, with cardiac enzymes on arrival and every 8 hours for 24 hours. Charts were abstracted with a closed-question instrument. Outcome: the proportion of admitted patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) by WHO criteria, plus in-hospital complications.
can_establish: How often adults admitted with chest pain after recent cocaine use at this one hospital in 1996–1998 met WHO enzyme criteria for myocardial infarction during a 24-hour rule-out (15 of 250), and how often in-hospital complications occurred and when.
cannot_establish: Whether cocaine caused the infarctions or the chest pain (no comparison group of patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine, and use at any time in the previous week was enough to enter); the risk of infarction for a person who uses cocaine (the denominator is admitted patients, not people who use cocaine); what predicts infarction (patients with and without infarction are never compared); or how many small infarctions CK-MB testing missed (the authors cannot exclude a few missed non-Q-wave infarctions, p. 877).

sample.recruitment: Records (clinic): computer-assisted search of medical records for all ED presentations from 1 July 1996 to 28 February 1998, cross-referencing ICD-9 codes for chest pain and myocardial infarction with the ICD-9 codes for cocaine and/or drug abuse (the coding categories searched), then checked against an ED log of all admitted patients (p. 874, Methods › Study Setting and Population).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included if aged 18 or older, with a chief complaint of anterior, precordial or left-sided chest discomfort lasting less than 12 hours, and either documented cocaine use in the week before presentation or a urine screen positive for cocaine or its metabolites (p. 874). Excluded: 9 patients discharged from the ED against the admission policy (pp. 874–875).
sample.demographics: Mean age 33.5 years (SD 8.5); 192 men (77%) and 58 women (23%); 208 African American (84%), 24 White (10%), 3 Hispanic (1%), 15 other or unknown (6%). Hypertension 26%, hypercholesterolaemia 8%, family history of coronary disease 34%, diabetes 6%, tobacco use 77%; previous chest pain 40%, previous myocardial infarction 6% (16), heart failure 2%, arrhythmia 1%; mean 1.5 (SD 1.1) traditional cardiac risk factors (Table 1, p. 874; Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 875).
sample.attrition: 9 of 259 identified patients (3.5%) were excluded because they had been discharged from the ED; they did not differ significantly in age, sex, ethnicity or cardiac risk factors, their complications are unknown, and all nine were alive at the end of the study period (pp. 874–875). None of the 250 admitted patients was lost; all survived to discharge (p. 875).
sample.selection_effects: One urban hospital whose patients were mostly young, male, African American and smoking crack; other settings are untested. Patients could enter only if their cocaine use was recorded in a way that produced the cocaine or drug-abuse codes, and urine toxicology was part of the cardiac work-up by policy only for patients aged 50 or under without traditional risk factors (p. 876), so cocaine use in older patients or patients with risk factors was less likely to be found; the authors concede some patients over 50 may have been missed (pp. 876–877). Case-finding was more thorough for the numerator than for the denominator: every chart coded for AMI, with or without cocaine, was reviewed (p. 876), whereas patients without AMI whose cocaine use was not coded could not be found. That asymmetry, like the exclusion of the 9 ED discharges, would tend to raise the proportion with AMI (editors' reading). Patients with ischaemic symptoms other than chest pain were not included (p. 876).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine use in the week before presentation as documented in the chart, or a positive urine screen. Urine toxicology was performed in 196 of 250 patients (78%); 185 were positive (94% of those tested) (p. 875, Results, 3rd paragraph). The authors assume the 6% who reported use but tested negative bought a mislabelled or heavily adulterated substance or presented after the assay's detection window (p. 877).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Amount not recorded. Timing (a precise history was available for all but 3 patients): last use within 24 hours in 193 (printed 78%) and within 4 hours in 57 (printed 22%) (p. 875); the abstract gives 77% within 24 hours (p. 873). Route: crack inhalation 91% in the Results (p. 875), but crack 85%, intravenous 2% and nasal 6% in the abstract (p. 873).
exposure.polysubstance: Not recorded or reported, apart from tobacco use (77%). Alcohol and other drugs are not mentioned.

comparison.controls: None. There is no group of patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine, and patients with and without AMI are not compared with each other.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Coronary anatomy, earlier cardiac testing, and the pattern and amount of cocaine use are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Chart abstraction with a previously described closed-question instrument (interrater reliability reported in an earlier study, ref. 12; the abstract says it had 119 items) (p. 874; abstract, p. 873). Cardiac isoenzymes on presentation and every 8 hours for 24 hours in every patient. AMI by WHO criteria: CK-MB at least twice the institutional normal value with a typical rise and fall; infarcts classed as Q-wave or non-Q-wave and by location on the ECG. The initial ECG was classed in a closed-question format as normal, nonspecific (including early repolarization), abnormal but not diagnostic of ischaemia, ischaemic (old, or not known to be old), or suggestive of AMI (p. 874).
outcomes.validity_norms: WHO criteria with serial CK-MB, the standard of the time. Every diagnosed AMI had CK-MB above 20 IU/L although the threshold was twice normal (10 IU/L); the authors therefore cannot exclude that a very small number of non-Q-wave infarctions were missed (p. 877).
outcomes.operationalization: AMI as above. Complications recorded with their timing during the stay: congestive heart failure, ventricular tachycardia, supraventricular tachydysrhythmias and bradydysrhythmias (p. 874).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive proportions without hypothesis tests; a 95% CI is given for the main outcome (AMI) only (p. 874).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to routine enzyme testing; whether chart abstractors knew the study question is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: AMI in 15 of 250 (6%); 95% CI printed as 3.1% to 8.9% in the Results (p. 875) and 4.1% to 8.9% in the abstract (p. 873). Editors' calculation: the Results interval is the normal-approximation (Wald) interval (3.06–8.94%); the exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% interval is 3.4% to 9.7%. Of the 15: initial ECG consistent with AMI in 9, ischaemic changes in 4, normal or nondiagnostic in 2; 8 anterior, 6 inferior, 1 indeterminate; 9 Q-wave (60%) (p. 875). Initial ECG in all 250: normal 67 (27%), nonspecific 125 (50%; 41 of them early repolarization), abnormal but nondiagnostic 33 (13%), ischaemia known to be old 6 (2%), ischaemia not known to be old 10 (4%), suggestive of AMI 9 (4%) (p. 875). Complications: bradydysrhythmia 1 (0.4%), heart failure 1 (0.4%), supraventricular tachycardia 3 (1.2%), sustained ventricular tachycardia 2 (0.8%); none more than 12 hours after ED arrival; no deaths before discharge (pp. 875–876). Coronary care unit: 24 patients, mean stay 2.7 days (SD 1.9); mean hospital stay for all 2.2 days (SD 2.0) (p. 875). Editors' calculation: no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients is compatible with a true rate of up to 1.5% (exact two-sided 95% interval 0 to 1.5%).
analysis.selective_reporting: Patients with and without AMI are not compared on age, risk factors, ECG, time since use or toxicology, although all were abstracted. Treatments given in hospital (for example nitrates, aspirin, beta-blockers, catheterization) are not reported. The abstract's description of the data instrument (119 items, high interrater reliability) refers to an instrument validated in an earlier study; no reliability was measured in this sample (pp. 873–874).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 15 events the exact 95% interval for the proportion runs from 3.4% to 9.7% (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 250 adults admitted with chest pain after recent cocaine use at one Michigan hospital in 1996–1998, 15 (6%) met WHO CK-MB criteria for myocardial infarction; complications were few (7 events), none occurred more than 12 hours after arrival, and no one died in hospital.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion call the 6% an incidence identical to that of prior prospective studies and say the study validates the COCHPA study (abstract, p. 873; Conclusions, p. 877); the last author also led COCHPA (ref. 11). Gaps: (1) 6% is the share of admitted patients, identified through cocaine or drug-abuse coding, whose enzymes met WHO criteria, not an incidence in people who use cocaine, and case-finding was more complete for infarctions than for non-infarctions (p. 876); (2) the uniform admission policy, which the authors say removes the selection bias of earlier studies (pp. 873, 876), addresses ED disposition but not the ascertainment of cocaine use, which depended on coding and on toxicology given mainly to patients aged 50 or under without risk factors; (3) the Discussion says the study confirms a previously suggested risk of 1.6 per 1,000 for adverse events after a 12-hour observation (p. 877), but zero events among 250 patients is compatible with a risk of up to about 15 per 1,000 (editors' calculation), so it cannot confirm a figure that small; (4) the abstract's interval (4.1–8.9%) differs from the Results (3.1–8.9%). The Discussion itself notes, about an earlier series, that an apparent cocaine–infarction association may reflect how common cocaine use is in the community rather than cause and effect (p. 876).

timeline.event: COCHPA, a prospective multicentre study of cocaine-associated chest pain at six municipal hospitals (Hollander et al., Acad Emerg Med 1994; ref. 11): AMI in 6%, criticized for low enrolment at some sites (as summarized on p. 876)
Same network's multicentre series of cocaine-associated myocardial infarction treated with or without thrombolysis (CAMI Study Group; last author of this paper is its first author)
Kontos et al. (ref. 5): AMI in 2.5% of a cohort of 241 patients with cocaine-associated chest pain and in 6 of 69 admitted to the coronary care unit (as summarized on p. 876)
This series: AMI in 15 of 250 admitted patients (6%) under a uniform admission policy

replication.where_it_stands: The 6% matches the authors' own earlier prospective multicentre estimate (COCHPA, 6%), with which it shares the last author, and the 5–6% of two prospective studies the authors cite; the retrospective series they cite ranged from 0% to 31% depending on whom they enrolled (p. 876). All of these come from CK-MB-era testing of patients who reached hospital with chest pain: the figure describes that presenting population and that test, not a risk per occasion of cocaine use. Primary studies cited here are not yet read and are named without ids.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Emergency Medicine at Hurley Medical Center (Flint, MI), the University of Michigan and the University of Pennsylvania (p. 873). The last author, Judd E. Hollander, led the COCHPA study (ref. 11) whose result this paper says it validates, and wrote the 12-hour observation work it says it confirms (refs 12, 18). The study was presented at the North American Congress of Clinical Toxicology in September 1997 (p. 873), before the stated study period ended (February 1998), so that presentation used part of the data.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multicentre cohort of all ED patients with chest pain who report cocaine use or test positive, with toxicology for everyone whatever their age, high-sensitivity troponin, and a comparison group of patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine, reporting the proportion with myocardial infarction and 30-day events by age, risk factors and time since use.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All admitted patients with cocaine-associated chest pain at one hospital, found through ICD-9 coding checked against the ED admission log; one urban centre, and capture of cocaine use depended on coding and on toxicology given mainly to patients aged 50 or under without risk factors.
Every eligible admission over 20 months under a uniform admission policy.
250 patients and 15 events; exact 95% interval 3.4–9.7% (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Setting, demographics, risk factors, presentation, vital signs and ECG categories reported (Tables 1–3, pp. 874–875).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 250 of 259 analysed; the 9 excluded ED discharges were probably at lower risk; infarctions were searched for through all AMI charts, while patients without AMI could be found only through cocaine coding.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: WHO criteria with serial CK-MB over 24 hours, the standard of the time; small non-Q-wave infarctions may have been missed (p. 877).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Enzymes on arrival and every 8 hours for 24 hours in every patient (p. 874).
A proportion with a normal-approximation interval; the abstract's lower limit (4.1%) differs from the Results (3.1%); exact interval 3.4–9.7% (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Record review; no participation was required.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI checklist has no overall algorithm; the editors summarize the risk as moderate. The outcome (WHO CK-MB criteria on serial testing in every patient) was measured uniformly, and the admission policy made the admitted population close to the whole ED population with this complaint. The main risk lies in case-finding: patients entered through coding of their cocaine use, toxicology was routine only for younger patients without risk factors, and infarctions were searched for more thoroughly than non-infarctions, which would tend to raise the proportion. The card may be cited for the share of admitted patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who met WHO infarction criteria at this hospital in 1996–1998 (15 of 250, 6%, exact 95% interval 3.4–9.7%), for the low complication rate with no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients, and for who these patients were; not for a risk of infarction per occasion of cocaine use, for causation, or for predictors of infarction.

key_findings.finding: Of 250 adults admitted with chest pain after recent cocaine use, 15 (6%) met WHO criteria for acute myocardial infarction on serial CK-MB testing over 24 hours; 95% CI printed as 3.1% to 8.9%.
key_findings.note: The abstract prints 4.1% to 8.9% (p. 873). Editors' calculation: 3.1–8.9% is the normal-approximation interval; the exact 95% interval is 3.4% to 9.7%.

key_findings.finding: Case-finding: 259 patients with cocaine-associated chest pain were identified by searching ICD-9 codes for chest pain or myocardial infarction crossed with codes for cocaine and/or drug abuse, checked against the ED log of admitted patients; 9 discharged from the ED against the admission policy were excluded, leaving 250.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Setting and Population (p. 874); Results, 1st paragraph (pp. 874–875)

key_findings.finding: Who the patients were: mean age 33.5 years (SD 8.5); 77% men; 84% African American; tobacco use 77%; hypertension 26%; previous myocardial infarction 6%; previous chest pain 40%.

Cocaine exposure: all patients reported use within 7 days or had cocaine metabolites in urine; urine toxicology was done in 196, of whom 185 (94%) were positive; last use within 24 hours in 193 (78%) and within 4 hours in 57 (22%); crack inhalation was the commonest route (91%).
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 77% within 24 hours and crack 85%, intravenous 2%, nasal 6% (p. 873). The two timing counts add up to the whole sample (193 + 57 = 250), which leaves no room for the 3 patients without a precise history or for use 1–7 days earlier, and 193 of 250 is 77.2%; the timing figures are approximate at best.

key_findings.finding: Initial ECG: normal in 67 (27%), nonspecific in 125 (50%; 41 with early repolarization), abnormal but nondiagnostic in 33 (13%), ischaemia known to be old in 6 (2%), ischaemia not known to be old in 10 (4%), suggestive of AMI in 9 (4%). Among the 15 infarctions, the initial ECG was consistent with AMI in 9, ischaemic in 4, and normal or nondiagnostic in 2.

Infarct characteristics: 8 anterior (53%), 6 inferior, 1 of indeterminate location; 9 Q-wave (60%); every patient diagnosed with AMI had at least one CK-MB value above twice the upper limit of normal.

In-hospital course: 24 patients were admitted first to the coronary care unit (mean stay 2.7 days, SD 1.9); mean hospital stay 2.2 days (SD 2.0); all 250 survived to discharge. Complications: bradydysrhythmia in 1 (0.4%), heart failure in 1 (0.4%), supraventricular tachycardia in 3 (1.2%), sustained ventricular tachycardia in 2 (0.8%); none occurred more than 12 hours after ED arrival.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients is compatible with a true rate of up to 1.5% (exact 95% upper limit).

key_findings.finding: By departmental policy, urine toxicology was part of the cardiac work-up only for patients aged 50 or under without traditional risk factors; the authors say some patients over 50 who had used cocaine may not have been captured, and that all charts coded for AMI, with or without cocaine, were reviewed to limit coding errors.
key_findings.locator: Limitations and Future Questions, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors cannot exclude that a very small number of non-Q-wave infarctions were missed: every diagnosed infarction had CK-MB above 20 IU/L, while the criterion was twice normal (10 IU/L).

Earlier estimates as summarized by the authors: retrospective series 0% to 31% (3 of 48 coronary care patients; 0 of 101 in monitored beds; 22 of 70 admitted patients); prospective studies 5–6% (COCHPA 6%); one imaging cohort 2.5% of 241.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; read the primary studies before citing them.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% CI for the main outcome is printed as 4.1% to 8.9% in the abstract (p. 873) and as 3.1% to 8.9% in the Results (p. 875).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Results interval is the normal-approximation interval for 15 of 250; the abstract's lower limit matches no standard method. Cite 15 of 250 with the exact interval 3.4–9.7% (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Route and timing differ between abstract and Results: crack 85% (abstract) against crack inhalation 91% (Results); 77% against 78% with use in the preceding 24 hours. The timing counts (193 within 24 hours, 57 within 4 hours) add up to 250 and their percentages to 100%, which cannot be right if 3 patients had no precise history and use up to 7 days earlier allowed entry.
reporting_issues.consequence: Time since last use and route can be cited only approximately: most patients had used within 24 hours, mostly by smoking crack.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 22 patients (11%) with other or unknown pain location, and the Results give 41 (34%) of the nonspecific ECGs (one hundred twenty-five, written in words) as showing early repolarization. Editors' arithmetic: 22 of 250 is 8.8%, the location percentages add to 102%, and 41 of 125 is 32.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Arithmetic slips with no effect on the main outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: Inclusion required anterior, precordial or left-sided chest discomfort (p. 874), but Table 2 lists 4 patients (2%) with right-sided pain only (p. 875).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the criterion was applied loosely or right-sided anterior pain was counted as anterior; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The design is called a retrospective cohort study in the Methods (p. 873) and a retrospective case series in the Discussion (p. 876); the study period is called 19 months (p. 876), but 1 July 1996 to 28 February 1998 is 20 months; men are 77% in the abstract and Table 1 (192 of 250) but 76% in the Discussion (p. 877).
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling and arithmetic slips; no effect on the main outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract credits the data instrument with 119 items and high interrater reliability (p. 873); the Methods cite the reliability from an earlier study (ref. 12) and no reliability was measured in this sample (p. 874).
reporting_issues.consequence: The reliability of chart abstraction in this study is unknown.
